gloss: To get something by paying money for it.
examples: You can *purchase* tickets online or at the door.
They *purchased* the building in 2019.
Anything *purchased* this week can be returned until Friday.
contrast: Stress the first syllable, PUR-chuhs; the second syllable is a schwa, not the word *chase*.

transitivity: both — transitive (order a pizza), intransitive (have you ordered yet?)
gloss: To ask a shop or a restaurant to supply something for you.
examples: I'd like to *order* the salmon.
She *ordered* two chairs from a catalog.
Your books have already been *ordered*.
contrast: You *order* something **from** a store or a company.

gloss: To go to stores looking for things to buy.
examples: We usually *shop* on Saturday mornings.
They *shopped* for a used car all weekend.
I hate *shopping* for clothes.
contrast: Double the *p*: *shopped*, *shopping*. You *shop* **for** what you are looking for.

transitivity: both — transitive (browse the catalog), intransitive (I'm just browsing)
gloss: To look at goods without planning to buy anything in particular.
examples: No thanks, I'm just *browsing*.
He *browsed* the shelves for twenty minutes.
Feel free to *browse* while I ring this up.

gloss: To pick one thing out of several.
examples: *Select* a payment method and click Continue.
She *selected* the cheapest shipping option.
The items you have *selected* are in your cart.

gloss: To arrange for something to be kept for you.
examples: I'd like to *reserve* a table for four.
We *reserved* the car online for Friday.
That seat is *reserved*.

transitivity: both — transitive (book a room), intransitive (book early and save)
gloss: To pay in advance to hold a seat, a room or a ticket.
examples: *Book* early and you'll pay half as much.
We *booked* the flight back in January.
The hotel is fully *booked* for the weekend.

gloss: To come to own something, especially by buying it.
examples: Big chains *acquire* small brands all the time.
The bank *acquired* three smaller lenders last year.
She has *acquired* quite a collection of old records.
contrast: Spelled with **cq**: *acquire*, not *aquire*.

gloss: To get something, especially with some effort or through an official process.
examples: You can *obtain* a refund within thirty days.
He *obtained* the parts from a dealer in Ohio.
The license was *obtained* legally.

ru: позволять себе, быть в состоянии купить
gloss: To have enough money for something.
examples: We can't *afford* a bigger apartment right now.
I could have *afforded* the trip if I hadn't bought the bike.
He works two jobs and still barely *affords* the rent.
contrast: Almost always with *can*, *can't*, *could* or *be able to*: *I can't afford it*, not *I don't afford it*.

gloss: To argue back and forth about a price until both sides agree.
examples: At the market you're expected to *haggle*.
He *haggled* over the price for an hour.
They spent the morning *haggling* with the dealer.
contrast: You *haggle* **over** a price **with** a seller.

gloss: To discuss terms with someone until you reach a price both sides accept.
examples: Tourists rarely *bargain*, so they pay more.
The union *bargained* for higher wages.
We're still *bargaining* over the price of the truck.
contrast: You *bargain* **with** a seller **for** or **over** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (negotiate a price), intransitive (negotiate with the seller)
gloss: To talk with someone in order to reach an agreement about money or terms.
examples: Dealers expect you to *negotiate*.
They *negotiated* a lower rent.
The contract is still being *negotiated*.
contrast: The **-ti-** is said *shee*: ni-GOH-shee-ayt.

gloss: To say that you are willing to give or pay something.
examples: They *offer* free shipping on orders over fifty dollars.
He *offered* me two hundred for the bike.
The store is *offering* ten percent off this week.
contrast: One *r*: *offered*, *offering*. The stress is on the first syllable, so the consonant is not doubled.

gloss: To decide what something will cost.
examples: They *price* everything a dollar under the competition.
The house was *priced* too high and sat for a year.
We're still *pricing* the new models.
contrast: Drop the *e* before *-ing*: *pricing*, not *priceing*.

gloss: To lower the price of something.
examples: Stores *discount* winter coats in February.
They *discounted* the sofa by thirty percent.
Everything on this rack is *discounted*.
contrast: As a verb you also hear dis-KOWNT; the noun (*a discount*) is always DIS-kownt.

gloss: To make an amount or a price smaller.
examples: We need to *reduce* costs before spring.
They *reduced* the price twice and it still didn't sell.
Prices have been *reduced* across the whole store.
contrast: American English says ri-DOOSS, without the *y*-sound of British ri-DYOOSS.

gloss: To make a price or an amount higher, or to collect money for a purpose.
examples: Landlords *raise* the rent almost every year.
They *raised* forty thousand dollars for the clinic.
Gas prices have been *raised* twice this month.
contrast: *Raise* always takes an object (*raise prices*); the verb with no object is the irregular *rise* (*prices rise*).

gloss: To make a price, a rate or an amount smaller.
examples: If they *lower* the price, I'll buy it.
The bank *lowered* our interest rate.
They're *lowering* fees to win customers back.

transitivity: both — transitive (increase the price), intransitive (sales increased)
gloss: To make something larger in amount, or to become larger.
examples: Shipping costs *increase* every year.
They *increased* the price of a ticket by five dollars.
Online sales have *increased* sharply since March.
contrast: The verb is in-KREESS, the noun IN-kreess — the stress moves.

gloss: To advertise and sell a product to a particular group of buyers.
examples: They *market* the phone to teenagers.
The drink was *marketed* as a health product.
She spent years *marketing* other people's books.
contrast: You *market* a product **to** the people you want to buy it.

transitivity: both — transitive (advertise a sale), intransitive (they advertise on the radio)
gloss: To tell the public about a product so that people will buy it.
examples: Small shops rarely *advertise* on TV.
The job was *advertised* in three papers.
They're *advertising* a huge sale this weekend.
contrast: Keeps **-ise** even in American spelling: *advertise*, never *advertize*.

gloss: To push a product or an event so that more people buy it or come.
examples: They *promote* the store with coupons in the mail.
The band *promoted* the album for a year.
The film is being *promoted* everywhere right now.

gloss: To put a new product on sale for the first time.
examples: They *launch* a new model every fall.
The company *launched* the product in June.
A cheaper version is being *launched* next month.

gloss: To sell something to whoever offers the most money.
examples: They *auction* the unclaimed bags twice a year.
The painting was *auctioned* for two million dollars.
He's *auctioning* his whole record collection online.

transitivity: both — transitive (trade stocks), intransitive (trade with Mexico)
gloss: To buy and sell goods, or to give one thing in exchange for another.
examples: The two countries *trade* mostly in oil and grain.
He *traded* his old truck for a van.
Shares were *trading* at forty dollars this morning.
contrast: You *trade* one thing **for** another, and *trade* **with** a partner.

gloss: To sell and send goods to another country.
examples: They *export* almost half of what they grow.
The company *exported* ten thousand units last year.
Most of the coffee is *exported* to Europe.
contrast: The verb is ik-SPORT, the noun EK-sport — the stress moves.

gloss: To buy goods from another country and bring them in.
examples: We *import* most of our fruit in winter.
The parts were *imported* from Korea.
They stopped *importing* steel after the tariff.
contrast: The verb is im-PORT, the noun IM-port.

gloss: To provide a business or a person with goods they need.
examples: Two farms *supply* the whole restaurant.
They *supplied* the paint and we did the work.
The store has been *supplied* by the same bakery for years.
contrast: *-y* after a consonant becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *supplies*, *supplied*.

ru: держать в продаже, иметь в ассортименте
gloss: To keep goods in a store so that customers can buy them.
examples: We don't *stock* that brand anymore.
They *stocked* the shelves before opening.
The store is well *stocked* for the holidays.

transitivity: both — transitive (restock the shelves), intransitive (we restock on Mondays)
gloss: To fill a store or a shelf again after the goods have been sold.
examples: They *restock* every Tuesday morning.
The shelves were *restocked* overnight.
We're *restocking* your size next week.

transitivity: both — transitive (deliver a package), intransitive (do they deliver?)
gloss: To bring goods to the person who bought them.
examples: Do they *deliver* on Sundays?
The couch was *delivered* a week late.
He's out *delivering* orders right now.
contrast: You *deliver* something **to** someone, at an address.

transitivity: both — transitive (ship an order), intransitive (it ships tomorrow)
gloss: To send goods to a customer by mail or freight.
examples: We *ship* anywhere in the country.
Your order *shipped* this morning.
The package is being *shipped* from Ohio.
contrast: Double the *p*: *shipped*, *shipping*.

gloss: To put goods into boxes or wrapping so they can be sold or sent.
examples: They *package* the cookies in threes.
The gift was *packaged* beautifully.
She spent the evening *packaging* orders.

gloss: To put a tag or a sticker on goods showing what they are or what they cost.
examples: *Label* every box before it goes out.
The jars were *labeled* by hand.
He's in the back *labeling* the new stock.
contrast: American English uses one *l*: *labeled*, *labeling*; British writes *labelled*, *labelling*.

gloss: To put goods where customers can see them.
examples: They *display* the sale items by the door.
The watches were *displayed* in a locked case.
She's *displaying* the new arrivals in the window.
contrast: *-y* after a vowel does not change: *displayed*, *displays* — unlike *supply* → *supplied*.

gloss: To put something up for sale, usually with a price.
examples: I'm going to *list* the bike online tonight.
She *listed* the house for four hundred thousand.
The item has been *listed* for a month with no offers.

transitivity: both — transitive (return a shirt), intransitive (return to the store)
gloss: To take something you bought back to the store and get your money back.
examples: You can *return* anything within thirty days.
She *returned* the shoes because they pinched.
Gifts bought in December can be *returned* until January 31.
contrast: You *return* something **to** the store. Don't say *return back*.

gloss: To give something back and take a different thing in its place.
examples: Can I *exchange* this for a larger size?
We *exchanged* dollars for pesos at the airport.
The sweater was *exchanged* twice before it fit.
contrast: You *exchange* one thing **for** another.

transitivity: both — transitive (swap seats), intransitive (want to swap?)
gloss: To give one thing and get another in return, with no money involved.
examples: Want to *swap* seats?
They *swapped* cars for the weekend.
We've been *swapping* tools all summer.
contrast: Double the *p*: *swapped*, *swapping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (barter eggs for wood), intransitive (they still barter)
gloss: To pay for goods or work with other goods or work instead of money.
examples: Some neighbors still *barter* instead of paying cash.
He *bartered* a week of carpentry for a used piano.
They were *bartering* eggs for firewood.

gloss: To give a customer back the money they paid.
examples: We'll *refund* your money if it breaks.
They *refunded* the shipping but not the item.
The deposit has already been *refunded*.
contrast: The verb is ri-FUND, the noun REE-fund.

gloss: To pay someone back money they spent on your behalf.
examples: The company will *reimburse* you for the gas.
They *reimbursed* me within a week.
Travel costs are *reimbursed* once a month.
contrast: You *reimburse* someone **for** an expense.

gloss: To pay what you owe in full and close the account.
examples: I'll *settle* the bill and meet you outside.
They *settled* the debt in full last month.
The claim was *settled* out of court.

transitivity: both — transitive (tip the driver), intransitive (Americans tip generously)
gloss: To give extra money to someone for service.
examples: Americans usually *tip* about twenty percent.
He *tipped* the driver ten dollars.
Nobody enjoys *tipping* at a counter.
contrast: Double the *p*: *tipped*, *tipping*.

ru: вносить на счёт, класть в банк
gloss: To put money into a bank account.
examples: You can *deposit* a check with your phone.
She *deposited* the money the same day.
The refund was *deposited* into my account on Friday.
contrast: You *deposit* money **into** an account.

gloss: To move money from one account or person to another.
examples: I'll *transfer* the money tonight.
She *transferred* two hundred dollars to his account.
The funds are still being *transferred*.
contrast: Double the *r*: *transferred*, *transferring* — the stress falls on the last syllable.

gloss: To send money electronically from one bank to another.
examples: Can you *wire* me the money today?
He *wired* two thousand dollars to the seller.
They're *wiring* the payment this afternoon.

gloss: To exchange a check for money.
examples: You can *cash* a check at any branch.
She *cashed* her paycheck on Friday.
He's at the bank *cashing* the check now.
contrast: Add *-es* after *-sh*: *cashes*.

gloss: To send someone a statement of what they owe.
examples: They *bill* customers at the end of the month.
The clinic *billed* my insurance directly.
You'll be *billed* twelve dollars a month.
contrast: You *bill* someone **for** something: *They billed me for two nights*.

gloss: To send a business a written bill for goods or work.
examples: We *invoice* clients every two weeks.
She *invoiced* them for forty hours.
The parts were *invoiced* separately.

transitivity: both — transitive (they overcharged me), intransitive (that shop overcharges)
gloss: To make someone pay more than the correct price.
examples: Restaurants near the airport *overcharge* for everything.
The garage *overcharged* us by a hundred dollars.
I think we're being *overcharged*.

gloss: To make people pay money to the government on goods, income or property.
examples: The state *taxes* restaurant meals.
They *taxed* the sale at eight percent.
Cigarettes are *taxed* heavily here.
contrast: Add *-es* after *-x*: *taxes*.

gloss: To make someone pay money as a punishment.
examples: They *fine* you fifty dollars for parking there.
He was *fined* two hundred for paying late.
The city has been *fining* landlords who ignore the rule.
contrast: Same spelling as the adjective *fine* (good), but here it means money paid as a punishment.

gloss: To add up to a certain amount, or to add figures up.
examples: The repairs *total* about nine hundred dollars.
Her purchases *totaled* forty-two dollars and change.
He's at the desk *totaling* up the receipts.
contrast: American English uses one *l*: *totaled*, *totaling*; British writes *totalled*, *totalling*.

gloss: To work out an amount using numbers.
examples: The site *calculates* shipping at checkout.
I *calculated* the tip in my head.
Interest is *calculated* monthly.

gloss: To say roughly what something will cost or how long it will take.
examples: They *estimate* the repair at six hundred dollars.
The contractor *estimated* three weeks of work.
Costs were *estimated* before the job started.
contrast: The verb is ES-tuh-mayt; the noun *an estimate* ends in a schwa, ES-tuh-mut.

gloss: To tell a customer the price you will charge.
examples: Call two plumbers and see what they *quote*.
The garage *quoted* me four hundred dollars.
We were *quoted* a much lower price last week.

gloss: To judge how much money something is worth.
examples: Insurers *value* the ring at ten thousand dollars.
The company was *valued* at two billion.
She *valued* the collection for the estate.

gloss: To examine something professionally and state its value.
examples: A specialist will *appraise* the painting.
The house was *appraised* at less than the asking price.
He *appraised* the jewelry in ten minutes.
contrast: Not the same word as *apprise* (uh-PRYZE), which means to inform someone.

gloss: To judge the value or amount of something, or to charge a fee officially.
examples: The county *assesses* property every three years.
They *assessed* a late fee of twenty dollars.
The damage is still being *assessed*.

gloss: To check someone's financial records officially.
examples: The IRS can *audit* returns up to three years old.
Their books were *audited* last spring.
An outside firm is *auditing* the accounts.

gloss: To make money coming in equal money going out in an account.
examples: She *balances* the register every night.
I finally *balanced* my checkbook.
The budget has to be *balanced* by June.

transitivity: both — transitive (budget two thousand dollars), intransitive (we budget carefully)
gloss: To plan how much money to spend on each thing.
examples: We *budget* about four hundred a month for food.
They *budgeted* two thousand dollars for the trip.
He has never been good at *budgeting*.
contrast: One *t*: *budgeted*, *budgeting*. You *budget* **for** an expense.

gloss: To spend less money than before.
examples: When the rent went up, we had to *economize*.
They *economized* by cooking at home every night.
She's been *economizing* since she lost her job.
contrast: American spelling **-ize**; British writes *economise*.

gloss: To use something carefully so that it lasts longer.
examples: Small shops have to *conserve* cash in the winter.
They *conserved* fuel by driving less.
The company is *conserving* money by not hiring.

gloss: To collect more and more of something over time.
examples: Points *accumulate* every time you shop.
He *accumulated* a small fortune in twenty years.
Debt had been *accumulating* for months before she noticed.
contrast: Two *c*'s and one *m*: *accumulate*.

gloss: To store up a large amount of money or goods and keep it hidden.
examples: Some people *hoard* cash at home.
Buyers *hoarded* lumber when prices jumped.
They've been *hoarding* supplies since the shortage.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *horde* (a crowd), but is spelled with an *a*.

gloss: To spend money on something useless.
examples: Don't *waste* money on the extended warranty.
We *wasted* three hundred dollars on a printer we never used.
He's *wasting* his savings on lottery tickets.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *waist* (the middle of the body).

gloss: To spend a lot of money on something you don't really need, as a treat.
examples: Once a year we *splurge* on a nice hotel.
She *splurged* on a leather jacket.
They're *splurging* a little for their anniversary.
contrast: You *splurge* **on** something.

gloss: To waste a large amount of money foolishly.
examples: He *squanders* every paycheck the week he gets it.
They *squandered* the inheritance in two years.
She had *squandered* a fortune before anyone noticed.

gloss: To provide the money that something needs.
examples: Donations *fund* most of the shelter's work.
The project was *funded* by the city.
They're *funding* the expansion out of profits.

gloss: To pay for something with borrowed money, or to supply the money for it.
examples: Most buyers *finance* a car over five or six years.
They *financed* the kitchen with a home equity loan.
The dealership is *financing* the whole purchase.
contrast: Also heard as fuh-NANSS; both are normal in American English.

gloss: To make money out of a deal or a situation.
examples: Resellers *profit* from every shortage.
He *profited* nicely when the stock split.
Nobody is *profiting* at these prices.
contrast: You *profit* **from** something, and the verb sounds exactly like *prophet*.

gloss: To get money by working for it.
examples: Servers *earn* most of their money in tips.
She *earned* four hundred dollars last weekend.
He's *earning* twice what he made before.
contrast: Sounds like *urn*. You *earn* money by working; you *win* it by luck.

transitivity: both — transitive (gain customers), intransitive (the stock gained)
gloss: To get more of something, or to rise in value.
examples: The fund *gains* about six percent a year.
The stock *gained* two dollars on Tuesday.
They have *gained* thousands of customers since the price cut.

gloss: To produce a profit or a return on money invested.
examples: Savings accounts *yield* almost nothing now.
The bonds *yielded* four percent last year.
That investment has *yielded* a steady income for a decade.

transitivity: both — transitive (diversify your savings), intransitive (investors should diversify)
gloss: To put money into several different things so that one loss cannot ruin you.
examples: Advisers always tell you to *diversify*.
She *diversified* her savings after the crash.
The firm is *diversifying* into groceries.
contrast: *-y* after a consonant becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *diversifies*, *diversified*.

gloss: To buy something risky hoping its price will rise.
examples: He *speculates* in farmland.
They *speculated* on oil and lost badly.
People were *speculating* in housing all through the boom.
contrast: You *speculate* **in** a market or **on** a price.

gloss: To have something as your legal property.
examples: They *own* three stores in the county.
He *owned* the building for thirty years.
The land has been *owned* by the same family since 1890.
contrast: A state, not an action: say *I own a car*, not *I am owning a car*.

gloss: To have something, especially as property.
examples: Almost nobody *possesses* enough cash to buy a house outright.
She *possessed* very little when she arrived.
Everything *possessed* by the company was sold to pay the debt.
contrast: The *ss* in the middle sounds like a *z*: puh-ZESS.

gloss: To have to pay money back to someone.
examples: I still *owe* you twenty bucks.
She *owed* the bank more than the car was worth.
Nobody knows how much is *owed* on the house.
contrast: The *w* is silent — the word rhymes with *go*. You *owe* someone **for** something.

gloss: To let someone use your money and expect it back.
examples: Banks won't *loan* money without collateral.
He *loaned* me four hundred dollars.
The money was *loaned* at six percent.
contrast: In American English *loan* is a normal verb; British speakers use *lend*. It sounds like *lone*.

gloss: To borrow money using your house or land as security.
examples: They had to *mortgage* the farm to keep it running.
The house was *mortgaged* twice.
He's *mortgaging* his future to pay for school.
contrast: The *t* is silent: MOR-gij.

gloss: To promise formally to give a sum of money.
examples: Listeners *pledge* money during the fundraiser.
The company *pledged* a million dollars to the school.
He's *pledging* ten dollars a month.

ru: сдавать или брать в аренду (по договору)
gloss: To use property or a car for a fixed period under a written contract, paying monthly.
examples: A lot of drivers *lease* instead of buying.
They *leased* the space for five years.
The car she's *leasing* costs three hundred a month.
contrast: It works both ways: the owner *leases* the space **to** you, and you *lease* it **from** them.

transitivity: both — transitive (rent an apartment), intransitive (the place rents for 900 a month)
gloss: To pay money to use something that belongs to someone else, or to let someone use yours for money.
examples: We *rent* a car whenever we fly.
They *rented* the cabin for a week.
The apartment has been *rented* to a student.
contrast: You *rent* something **from** the owner and *rent* it **to** a tenant.

gloss: To pay someone to do work for you.
examples: They *hire* extra drivers every December.
We *hired* a lawyer to read the contract.
The store is *hiring* for the holidays.
contrast: In American English *hire* is about people; for things Americans say *rent a car*, where the British say *hire a car*.

gloss: To take in money that people owe or give.
examples: The landlord *collects* rent on the first.
They *collected* four thousand dollars at the door.
Sales tax is *collected* by the state.

gloss: To get something that is sent or given to you.
examples: You'll *receive* a receipt by email.
We *received* the package on Monday.
She has *received* two refunds this month.
contrast: *i* before *e* except after *c*: *receive*, not *recieve*.

gloss: To ask for money that you have a right to, such as an insurance payment or a prize.
examples: You can *claim* the damage on your insurance.
He *claimed* the prize a week later.
The money was never *claimed*.

gloss: To exchange a coupon, a voucher or points for goods or money.
examples: You can *redeem* the coupon at any branch.
She *redeemed* her points for a flight.
The gift card has already been *redeemed*.

gloss: To give money or goods to a charity or a cause.
examples: They *donate* a dollar from every sale.
He *donated* his old suits to a shelter.
People have been *donating* all week.
contrast: You *donate* something **to** an organization.

gloss: To pay for an event or a team, usually in exchange for advertising.
examples: Local businesses *sponsor* the team.
The race was *sponsored* by a bank.
They're *sponsoring* the food drive again this year.

gloss: To pay part of the cost of something so that others pay less.
examples: The state *subsidizes* bus fares for students.
Housing was *subsidized* for low-income families.
Taxpayers are *subsidizing* the whole project.
contrast: American spelling **-ize**; British writes *subsidise*.

gloss: To set aside a sum of money for a particular purpose.
examples: They *allocate* ten percent of the budget to repairs.
The city *allocated* two million for new buses.
Funds are *allocated* every January.

gloss: To send goods out to stores, or to divide money among people.
examples: One company *distributes* the brand across the whole region.
Profits were *distributed* among the partners.
They're *distributing* free samples at the entrance.

gloss: To stop an order, a booking or a subscription before it takes effect.
examples: You can *cancel* the subscription any time.
They *canceled* the order before it shipped.
My card was *canceled* after the fraud.
contrast: American English uses one *l* in *canceled*, *canceling*, but two in the noun *cancellation*.

gloss: To pay again so that a contract or a subscription continues.
examples: I have to *renew* the lease in March.
She *renewed* the membership for another year.
The policy is *renewed* automatically every fall.
contrast: American ri-NOO, not the British ri-NYOO.

ru: повышать класс, переходить на более дорогой вариант
transitivity: both — transitive (upgrade your plan), intransitive (we upgraded at the gate)
gloss: To pay more for a better version of what you already have.
examples: For ten dollars more you can *upgrade* to the larger size.
We *upgraded* our seats at the gate.
The software has been *upgraded* twice this year.
contrast: The verb is up-GRAYD, the noun UP-grayd.

transitivity: both — transitive (register a car), intransitive (register online)
gloss: To put a purchase or an owner on an official list.
examples: *Register* the product to get the extra year of warranty.
They *registered* the truck in Nevada.
Have you *registered* your card for the discount?

gloss: To promise that something will happen or that goods will be repaired if they fail.
examples: They *guarantee* the price for thirty days.
The seller *guaranteed* the repair for a year.
Delivery isn't *guaranteed* before Christmas.
contrast: Silent *u* after the *g*, and the stress falls on the last syllable: ga-ruhn-TEE.

gloss: To give official permission to sell something, or to let a company use your name or design for money.
examples: The state *licenses* every dealer.
The design was *licensed* to a toy company.
They're *licensing* the name to three manufacturers.
contrast: American English spells the noun and the verb the same, *license*; British spells the noun *licence*.

gloss: To come to the end of the period when it can be used.
examples: The coupon *expires* on Sunday.
My card *expired* last month.
The warranty is *expiring* in two weeks.

gloss: To give someone money or a benefit for what they have done.
examples: The card *rewards* you with points on every purchase.
They *rewarded* loyal customers with a discount.
Regular buyers are *rewarded* with free shipping.
contrast: You *reward* someone **for** something, usually **with** something.

gloss: To change money from one currency into another.
examples: The app *converts* dollars to euros instantly.
We *converted* the last of our cash at the airport.
Prices are *converted* at yesterday's rate.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-VURT, the noun KAHN-vurt.

gloss: To pass a bank card through a machine to pay.
examples: *Swipe* your card and enter the PIN.
She *swiped* the card twice by mistake.
He was still *swiping* when the machine froze.

gloss: To read a barcode or a code with a machine.
examples: The register *scans* the barcode and adds the price.
She *scanned* the coupon at checkout.
He's *scanning* the items himself.
contrast: Double the *n*: *scanned*, *scanning*.

gloss: To handle a payment or an order through the necessary steps.
examples: The bank *processes* payments overnight.
They *processed* my refund in two days.
Your order is being *processed* right now.
contrast: American English says PRAH-sess; the British say PROH-sess.

gloss: To state definitely that an order, a booking or a payment is correct.
examples: Please *confirm* your order by email.
They *confirmed* the payment the same afternoon.
The booking has been *confirmed*.

gloss: To give official permission for a payment or a charge.
examples: Your bank has to *authorize* the charge.
She *authorized* the payment by phone.
The card was never *authorized* for that amount.
contrast: American spelling **-ize**; British writes *authorise*.

gloss: To agree to take money, a card or an offer.
examples: We don't *accept* checks.
They *accepted* my offer the same day.
Cards are *accepted* almost everywhere now.
contrast: Don't confuse it with *except* (not including); the two sound almost the same.

transitivity: both — transitive (decline an offer), intransitive (sales declined)
gloss: To refuse a card or an offer, or to go down in amount.
examples: Some stores *decline* foreign cards.
My card was *declined* at the gas station.
Sales have been *declining* since the new mall opened.

gloss: To officially give out a card, a refund or a document.
examples: The store will *issue* a store credit, not cash.
They *issued* the refund on Tuesday.
A new card is being *issued* to you.
contrast: American English says ISH-oo; the British often say IS-yoo.

gloss: To decide not to charge a fee or not to insist on a right.
examples: Some banks *waive* the fee if you keep a balance.
They *waived* the delivery charge because we complained.
The late fee was *waived* once as a courtesy.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *wave*, but *waive* means to give up a fee or a right.

gloss: To officially charge a tax, a fee or a fine.
examples: The city *levies* a small tax on hotel rooms.
They *levied* an extra charge on late payments.
A fine was *levied* against the company.
contrast: *-y* after a consonant becomes *-ies* and *-ied*: *levies*, *levied*.

transitivity: both — transitive (refinance the mortgage), intransitive (we refinanced last year)
gloss: To replace a loan with a new one, usually at a lower rate.
examples: Rates dropped, so a lot of people are trying to *refinance*.
They *refinanced* the house at a lower rate.
The loan has been *refinanced* twice.

gloss: To leave something valuable at a shop in exchange for money you can repay to get it back.
examples: He'll *pawn* the guitar if rent is short.
She *pawned* her ring to cover the bill.
The watch has been *pawned* and bought back twice.

gloss: To receive money or property from someone who has died.
examples: She'll *inherit* the store when her father retires.
He *inherited* forty thousand dollars and spent it in a year.
They're *inheriting* a business that owes money to everyone.

transitivity: both — transitive (double the price), intransitive (the rent doubled)
gloss: To make an amount twice as large, or to become twice as large.
examples: Shipping costs can *double* around the holidays.
The rent *doubled* in six years.
They're *doubling* the size of the store.

gloss: To ask for something firmly, as something you have a right to.
examples: Customers *demand* free returns these days.
She *demanded* a refund and got one.
They're *demanding* payment up front.
contrast: American di-MAND has the *a* of *cat*, not the British di-MAHND.

gloss: To ask politely or formally for something.
examples: You can *request* a refund through the app.
He *requested* an itemized bill.
We're *requesting* a copy of the receipt.
